name: Doro wat
subtitle: The ceremonial heart of Ethiopian cuisine: tender chicken pieces and hard-boiled eggs slow-braised for hours in caramelized red onions, spiced butter and berbere.

facts.label: Key spice
facts.value: Berbere (chilli, korarima Ethiopian cardamom, fenugreek, rue, garlic)

facts.label: Signature cooking fat
facts.value: Niter kibbeh (clarified spiced butter infused with sacred herbs)

parts.text: Doro wat is the crown jewel of Ethiopian and Eritrean festive cuisine, reserved for major religious celebrations such as Fasika (Easter), Genna (Christmas), and wedding banquets.

The preparation begins by dry-sweating mounds of finely minced red onions in a heavy clay pot for hours without oil until they break down into a luscious, mahogany-colored paste; only then are generous scoops of niter kibbeh (clarified spiced butter) and deep red berbere spice blend stirred in.
Tender pieces of chicken and whole hard-boiled eggs scored with a knife are slow-simmered in the velvety, deeply aromatic sauce until the spices infuse every bite.
Doro wat is ladled directly into the center of a wide woven basket table (messob) lined with sheets of tangy, spongy injera bread.

Guests tear off pieces of injera with the right hand to pinch up the chicken and sauce. A traditional host demonstrates affection and honor through 'gursha': tearing off a choice morsel of meat wrapped in injera and placing it directly into the mouth of a beloved guest or family elder.

sections.title: The rhythm of fast and feast

parts.text: In the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo calendar, faithful Christians observe over 180 fasting days per year (such as the 55-day Great Lent), eating an exclusively vegan diet free from all meat, poultry, dairy, and eggs.

When the midnight Easter liturgy concludes, the fast is broken at dawn with Doro Wat: the chicken, traditionally carved into precisely twelve ritual pieces representing the twelve apostles, celebrates the return of richness and communal life.

blocks.title: Authentic Ethiopian Doro Wat
blocks.sub: Classic slow-caramelized method adapted from chef Marcus Samuelsson and Ethiopian culinary historians.
blocks.note: Patience is essential: red onions must be cooked slowly without burning to build natural sweetness; ghee infused with cardamom and fenugreek can substitute for niter kibbeh.

ingredients.name: red onions, pureed or minced extremely fine
chicken drumsticks and thighs, skinless and slashed with a knife
hard-boiled eggs, peeled and scored with shallow cuts
garlic cloves, minced to a smooth paste with fresh ginger
fresh lemon juice for marinating the chicken

steps.text: Toss chicken pieces in lemon juice and salt, setting aside for 20 minutes to tenderize.
Place the pureed red onions into a dry, heavy Dutch oven over medium-low heat; cook for 35 minutes, stirring frequently until the moisture evaporates and the onions turn deep reddish-brown.
Add the niter kibbeh, garlic-ginger paste, and berbere spice, sautéing over low heat for 10 minutes until an intoxicating, glossy aroma develops.
Pour in warm chicken broth, add the marinated chicken pieces, cover, and simmer on gentle heat for 35 minutes until the chicken is tender to the bone.
Add the hard-boiled eggs, spooning the thick sauce over them; simmer gently for 10 minutes so the eggs absorb the deep red hue and spices.
Let rest for 15 minutes off heat so the butter rises to the surface, then serve in a platter atop fresh injera.

gaps: Regional disputes between the hot, intensely spiced Addis Ababa court-style doro wat and milder northern versions in Gojjam and Gondar.
The traditional heirloom varieties of korarima (false cardamom) and kosseret herbs required for authentic niter kibbeh, which are difficult to source outside the Ethiopian highlands.
